opus-5.5.text:
I think the main question I ask is: if this research goes well, does it actually change what we do in the world where things are dangerous? A lot of empirical work is interesting, and it produces nice papers, but the outcome doesn't really bear on the decisions we'll face when models are capable enough that alignment failures are catastrophic. So I try to trace the line from "we learned X" to "a lab, or a regulator, or a future researcher does something different because of X."

Concretely, a few things I look for. First, is the work studying a problem that we expect to get harder as systems get more capable, rather than one that will naturally go away with scale? If a failure mode gets fixed by just training bigger models with more data, it's not where I'd want marginal effort. The things I care most about are cases where the model might know something we don't, or might be optimizing for something that looks good to us rather than something that is good. Those don't obviously get easier.

Second, is there a plausible story for why the empirical setting is analogous to the real risk? There's always a gap between a toy setting and the thing you're worried about. That's fine, you have to start somewhere, but I want people to be explicit about what the analogy is and where it might break. A lot of the value of something like a "model organism" of deceptive behavior is in how carefully you've argued that it shares the relevant structure.

Third, does the research produce techniques or measurements that would still be useful if our theoretical picture turns out to be wrong? I like work that gives us better tools for noticing problems, like evaluations, interpretability that actually lets you check a claim, ways to measure whether oversight is working, because those buy robustness against our own confusion.

And then there's a more practical filter: is this something that wouldn't happen anyway? Some empirical alignment work lines up neatly with commercial incentives. Making models more helpful and less annoying is going to get done regardless. I'm more excited about the work that addresses risks that are hard to see in today's products, because that's where you'd expect underinvestment.

I'll admit these standards are pretty fuzzy in practice. I've been wrong about which directions would pan out, and a lot of valuable work looked kind of unpromising up front. So I try to hold them as heuristics for prioritizing rather than as a reason to dismiss things.

r001.rationale: The response offers practical heuristics for evaluating research, but does not argue that empirical alignment rationales are simple enough to evaluate on their face.

r002.rationale: It says the standards are fuzzy and that promising work can look unpromising, but does not address whether an apparently insurmountable obstacle is insufficient grounds to dismiss a research direction.

r003.rationale: It treats a lack of connection to consequential real-world decisions as a reason the work is not worth prioritizing, and asks researchers to show how the problem relates to real risks.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose comparing a field’s rate of progress with the total investment it has received.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the main thing I'm asking is: does this research actually bear on the problem we're ultimately going to face? Which is a really hard question, because the systems we're worried about don't exist yet. So you're always working with some proxy, and the question is how good the proxy is.

I'd break it down into a few things. The first is whether the work is on the path to a solution that actually scales. A lot of empirical alignment work is very reasonable stuff, like making current models more helpful or less likely to say offensive things, but it's pretty unclear that the techniques are going to keep working when models are much smarter than the people evaluating them. So I care a lot about whether there's a story for why this generalizes, or at least whether the research is set up to tell you when it stops working. If you're doing RLHF-style work, the interesting part to me isn't that you can get the model to do what you want today, it's whether you learn anything about what happens when the human can't tell whether the model did a good job.

The second thing is whether the experiment can actually fail. I think a lot of alignment research, both theoretical and empirical, is structured in a way where any result gets interpreted as confirming the approach. So I want to know in advance: what would I see that would make me think this direction is a dead end? If there's no answer to that, the research is more like demonstration than science, and demonstrations are fine, but they shouldn't update us very much.

And third, I think about whether it's building the kind of infrastructure or understanding the field will need regardless of which particular technical story turns out right. Things like being able to evaluate whether a model is deceiving you, or having good benchmarks for oversight when the task is too hard for the overseer, those seem useful across a lot of different scenarios. So even if I'm skeptical of the specific hypothesis, I'll often think work is worth doing because it builds capacity that we'll want later.

I'd also say I've gotten more sympathetic to empirical work over time, partly because I've seen how much theory alone has struggled to make contact with actual systems. So my bar isn't "this clearly solves the problem." It's more like: is there a plausible chain from this experiment to a decision someone would make differently, either about what to build or about how confident to be. If I can't draw that chain, I'm pretty skeptical. If I can, I'll often think it's worth doing even if the chain is kind of long.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether proxies and experiments connect to future alignment problems, but does not argue that empirical research rationales are simple enough to evaluate on their face.

r002.rationale: The response notes that the systems of concern do not yet exist and favors some research despite uncertainty, but does not say that an apparently insurmountable obstacle is insufficient reason to dismiss a research direction.

r003.rationale: The response is skeptical when it cannot trace an experiment to a decision, but does not identify lacking a plausible case for the problem's importance as grounds to reject work on it.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose comparing a field's rate of progress with the total investment it has received.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing I’m looking for is a story about how the research bears on the problem we ultimately care about. What uncertainty are you trying to resolve, and how would resolving it change what we do to align a much more capable system?

That doesn’t mean you need to work with systems that already exhibit the problems we’re worried about. You can study a simplified setting. But then a lot of the work is in making the argument that the simplification preserves the thing that matters. If your technique works because the model is less capable than the person supervising it, that’s a pretty significant limitation if the intended application is supervising models that understand the task much better than we do.

I also care about whether the experiment could surprise you. Is there a plausible result that would make you substantially less optimistic about your approach? If every possible outcome can be interpreted as progress, then it’s hard to learn very much.

So I’m generally more excited about an experiment that distinguishes between two plausible explanations of why something works than one that just makes a benchmark number go up. Improving the number can be useful, but I want to understand what we’ve learned and why we expect that lesson to carry over.

r001.rationale: The response asks for a rationale connecting research to alignment, but does not argue that empirical research rationales are simple enough to evaluate on their face.

r002.rationale: It notes limitations of simplified settings, but does not say that an apparently insurmountable obstacle is insufficient reason to dismiss a research direction.

r003.rationale: The response asks how research bears on alignment, but does not clearly state that lacking a plausible case for the problem’s importance is grounds to reject work on it.

r004.rationale: It does not propose comparing a field’s rate of progress with the total investment it has received.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main question is: what could you learn from this experiment that would change what you do? If the experiment goes well, does that give you a reason to use some particular training procedure? If it goes badly, would you abandon that procedure, or identify a problem you can then work on?

One concern I have is that you can do an experiment with current models, get a reassuring result, and still have essentially the same uncertainty about what happens when models are much smarter. So I want some account of why the thing you’re measuring now is informative about the problem you ultimately care about. It doesn’t have to settle that problem, but there should be an argument connecting the two.

For example, you might study whether a weak supervisor can train a stronger model to do something the supervisor can’t directly evaluate. You can construct settings where you know the right answer, restrict what the supervisor can see, and ask which methods recover good performance. That seems useful because you can test competing explanations for why a method works and find circumstances where it fails.

I wouldn’t insist that every project have an immediate application to a very powerful AI. A lot of useful research is exploratory. But I’d like the researcher to be able to say what uncertainty they’re trying to resolve, why it matters, and what different outcomes of the experiment would tell them.

r001.rationale: The response asks what an experiment could teach and how it connects to the larger problem, but does not argue that empirical alignment research rationales are simple enough to evaluate on their face.

r002.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about whether current-model results generalize, but does not address whether an apparently insurmountable obstacle is enough to dismiss a research direction.

r003.rationale: The response says researchers should explain why an uncertainty matters, but does not state that a missing plausible case for a problem’s importance is grounds to reject work on it.

r004.rationale: The response does not propose comparing a field’s rate of progress with the total investment it has received.
